protocol.legal_basis: Medicines and Poisons Regulations 2016 (WA): 'This clinical practice guideline may only be used by pharmacists who have been approved by the Department of Health to participate in the Enhanced Access Community Pharmacy Pilot (EACPP) and are authorised to prescribe under the Medicines and Poisons Regulations 2016 (WA). This document alone does not provide an authorisation for a pharmacist to prescribe.' (p.1)
protocol.supervision_model: Approved/authorised pharmacist prescribing under the EACPP (document's own terminology) with collaborative care: 'Pharmacists must exercise professional discretion and judgement consistent with their qualifications and legislative authority. This guideline does not override the responsibility of the pharmacist to undertake clinical assessments and to make decisions appropriate to the circumstances of the individual and the relevant standards of care, in consultation with the patient and/or their parent/caregiver.' (p.1). Entry Point 1 (possible but no previous diagnosis) permits pharmacotherapy only to Level 1 or 2 with concurrent referral, and 'Further program participation is not permitted until spirometry has been performed and collaborative management with a medical practitioner has been established.' (p.3)
protocol.scope_summary: EACPP clinical practice protocol for the Improved Asthma Symptom Control Program, community-based service for patients with asthma symptoms or an existing diagnosis of asthma, aged 16 to 65 years. Two entry points (p.3): Entry Point 1 - possible but no previous diagnosis, manage with non-pharmacological measures and pharmacotherapy to Level 1 or 2 only with concurrent referral until spirometry and collaborative care are established; Entry Point 2 - existing diagnosis, commence ongoing monitoring and management. Flow (p.6-7): eligibility -> history -> physical examination -> spirometry (conduct/interpret) -> assess symptom control -> commence collaborative care -> management plan (non-pharmacological plus pharmacotherapy Levels 1-3 per the 2025 Australian Asthma Handbook) -> confirm management appropriate -> communicate plan (written Asthma Action Plan) -> collaborative care -> clinical review. Page 4 lists 25 ineligibility criteria, page 5 four treat-and-concurrently-refer criteria, pages 17-18 cover exacerbation self-management including pharmacist-initiated prednis(ol)one, and page 19 lists indications for review by an appropriate healthcare provider.

inclusion.text: Confirm the patient does not meet any ineligibility criteria (refer to page 4).

Entry Point 1: Patients with possible but no previous diagnosis of asthma, who do not meet any ineligibility criteria, may be enrolled in the program and commence management (with non-pharmacological measures and pharmacotherapy to Level 1 or 2 only, if indicated) with concurrent referral to an appropriate healthcare provider for further review and collaborative care. Further program participation is not permitted until spirometry has been performed and collaborative management with a medical practitioner has been established.

Entry Point 2: Patients with an existing diagnosis of asthma, who do not meet any ineligibility criteria, may be enrolled in the program and commence ongoing monitoring and management (with non-pharmacological measures and pharmacotherapy, if indicated). An update must be provided to the patient's usual healthcare provider following each occasion of care.
Provide program overview, gain consent and enrol in program.
Document informed consent from the patient for participation, as per the Pilot Handbook.

This clinical practice guideline may only be used by pharmacists who have been approved by the Department of Health to participate in the Enhanced Access Community Pharmacy Pilot (EACPP) and are authorised to prescribe under the Medicines and Poisons Regulations 2016 (WA). This document alone does not provide an authorisation for a pharmacist to prescribe.

Consider program eligibility at every consultation, as eligibility may change at any time. Refer the patient to their usual healthcare provider with a comprehensive clinical handover if the patient is, or becomes, ineligible for management under the program.

diagnosis_pathways.name: Improved Asthma Symptom Control Program - guideline overview flow (pages 6-7), elaborated pages 9-19

steps.description: Patient eligibility for the program: 'Patient aged 16 to 65 years'; 'Confirm the patient does not meet any ineligibility criteria (refer to page 4)'. Refer when: 'the patient is aged below 16 or above 65 years (does not preclude a patient from accessing usual pharmacy care)' or 'if they are, or become, ineligible for the program'.

gates.criterion: Patient aged 16 to 65 years
Patient does not meet any of the ineligibility criteria on page 4

steps.description: Provide program overview, gain consent and enrol in program (overview content listed under 'There are 2 entry points for enrolment in the program' includes programme aims, expected outcomes, timeframes and costs, medicine management, other interventions, and the patient may leave the program at any time). Document informed consent from the patient for participation, as per the Pilot Handbook.

gates.criterion: Informed consent from the patient for participation documented as per the Pilot Handbook

steps.description: Take a detailed patient history. Including: patient characteristics; symptoms (current and history); medical history (consider contraindications to spirometry and conditions that impact asthma management/control); lifestyle/social/family history; review previous lung function test results (if available); most recent asthma action plan (if applicable).

Patient history (detailed): 'Obtain sufficient information to assess the safety and appropriateness of any recommendations and medicines.' Consider: age; ethnic or cultural background, including Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander status; lactation status; previous and current medical conditions including systemic and/or chronic conditions (refer to Appendix 2; consider contraindications to spirometry); previous diagnosis of asthma (date of diagnosis, last medical review, previous lung function test results, current or most recently prescribed treatment, previous use of oral corticosteroids, frequency of rapid-acting bronchodilator use (i.e. SABA or ICS-formoterol), most recent Asthma Action Plan); history of acute asthma and asthma exacerbations, including hospitalisations and ED visits; personal and/or family history of asthma or allergies; specialist care for any respiratory condition; previous and current respiratory symptoms (onset and severity, pattern, impact on daily activities including sleep and exercise); triggers, aggravating and precipitating factors (Appendix 4); relieving factors e.g. rapid-acting bronchodilator use; alarm signs and symptoms that require further investigation e.g. haemoptysis, chest pain, unexplained weight loss or gain, night sweats, fever, signs of bronchiectasis, recurrent pneumonia, orthopnoea, or oedema; all current and recently ceased treatments; drug and non-drug allergies, and adverse drug reactions; smoking status and history; home and work environment; diet/nutrition status and weight; levels of physical activity; recreational or illicit drug use and alcohol use; vaccination status (particularly COVID, influenza, RSV, pneumococcal, and pertussis).

gates.criterion: No alarm signs and symptoms that require further investigation (haemoptysis, chest pain, unexplained weight loss or gain, night sweats, fever, signs of bronchiectasis, recurrent pneumonia, orthopnoea, or oedema)

steps.description: Conduct physical examination - including chest auscultation.

Perform a physical examination (including chest auscultation and an inspection of the upper respiratory tract) to check for signs that suggest a comorbid or an alternative diagnosis. Consider: wheeze (widespread expiratory wheeze is suggestive of asthma but is not specific; wheeze may be absent in asthma; inspiratory wheeze is not a feature of asthma); presence of heart murmurs; crackles are not a feature of asthma (presence suggests another diagnosis, even if possibly co-existing with asthma). Look for signs of allergic rhinitis, nasal polyps, or rhinosinusitis in the upper respiratory tract; look for signs of atopic dermatitis. 'If COPD is suspected, the patient should be referred to a medical practitioner for further management.'

gates.criterion: Physical examination does not suggest a comorbid or an alternative diagnosis (e.g. crackles, heart murmurs, inspiratory wheeze, features of COPD)

steps.description: Conduct (or refer for) spirometry testing. 'Spirometry is required for a patient with suspected asthma, who has not been previously diagnosed, to confirm variable expiratory airflow limitation.' Spirometry is also recommended for a patient with an existing diagnosis of asthma: at initial presentation to establish baseline performance; if variable respiratory symptoms are reported but there is no available documented variable airflow limitation; if they have poor symptom control or have been experiencing exacerbations; after 3 to 6 months of using ICS containing treatment to establish a personal best for future comparison; as part of routine periodic review (approximately every 2 years) to assess risk of exacerbations and decline in lung function. Pharmacists may conduct spirometry in the community pharmacy setting in accordance with National Asthma Council Australia Spirometry Handbook for Primary Care if appropriately trained with appropriate equipment and quality assurance and audit processes; alternatively refer to an appropriate healthcare provider that performs lung function testing. Do not delay asthma treatment if clinically indicated while awaiting spirometry: if the patient does not have a prior diagnosis of asthma and asthma is suspected, therapy should be limited to Level 1 or Level 2 treatment only and spirometry performed within 3 months; an Asthma Action Plan should not be prepared if diagnosis has not been confirmed on spirometry; oral corticosteroids should not be supplied as part of an Asthma Action Plan before spirometry is performed that supports a diagnosis of asthma.

gates.criterion: Spirometry performed (or referred for) in accordance with the Spirometry Handbook; for suspected asthma without prior diagnosis spirometry performed within 3 months

steps.description: If the patient presents with acute respiratory symptoms that suggest an asthma exacerbation without a previous diagnosis (Entry Point 1), the patient must be referred to their usual healthcare provider (or emergency services, if required) before they can enter the program. Standard pharmacy care may be provided. If the patient has a previous diagnosis of asthma these should be managed as Management and treatment and investigations (including spirometry) performed after resolution of acute symptoms.

gates.criterion: Acute respiratory symptoms that suggest an asthma exacerbation are present in a patient without a previous diagnosis (Entry Point 1)

steps.description: Interpret spirometry (if applicable). Consider results in context of patient history and physical examination. Spirometry findings consistent with variable expiratory limitation include: positive bronchodilator responsiveness test - clinically significant FEV1 increase of >= 200 mL and >= 12 per cent from baseline pre-bronchodilator result (10 to 15 minutes after bronchodilator), or in those not already using ICS - clinically significant increase in pre-bronchodilator FEV1 (>= 200 mL and >= 12 per cent) measured before and after 4 weeks of maintenance inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) (or ICS-long acting beta2 agonist (LABA)) treatment. Refer the patient to their usual healthcare provider with a comprehensive clinical handover if spirometry results: do not demonstrate reversible airflow limitation or expiratory airflow limitation; suggest abnormal restrictive or mixed ventilatory patterns; are inconsistent with asthma (or difficult to interpret).

gates.criterion: Spirometry results demonstrate variable expiratory airflow limitation consistent with asthma
Spirometry results are interpretable and not unexpected for asthma

steps.description: Interpret spirometry testing in accordance with the current online version of the Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory (Pulmonary function testing - Spirometry) and the National Asthma Council Australia Spirometry Handbook for Primary Care (see Appendix 5). 'Any uncertainty on interpretation should be referred to a medical practitioner for review.' 'There is no single conclusive test for asthma. Diagnosis is based on patient history, physical examination, and spirometry. A diagnosis of asthma can be made if all the following apply: the patient has a history of recurrent or persistent respiratory symptoms that vary in frequency and severity; the patient's signs and symptoms are unlikely to be due to an alternative diagnosis; variable expiratory airflow limitation is demonstrated (and/or elevated fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) if testing is available).'

gates.criterion: Interpretation of spirometry is certain and diagnosis of asthma is confirmed (history of recurrent or persistent respiratory symptoms, unlikely alternative diagnosis, variable expiratory airflow limitation demonstrated)

steps.description: Assess symptom control. 'Assess and document symptom control throughout the program at every review.' Asthma symptom control can be assessed using the Australian Asthma Handbook - Classification of recent asthma symptom control in adults and adolescents or a validated questionnaire (see Appendix 6). Classification is based on symptoms over the previous 4 weeks: good control = all of daytime symptoms on 2 or fewer days per week, need for reliever on 2 or fewer days per week, no limitation of activities, no symptoms during night or on waking; poor control = any of daytime symptoms on more than 2 days per week, need for reliever on more than 2 days per week, any limitation of activities, any symptoms during night or on waking. An ACT score >= 20 indicates asthma may be well controlled; an ACT score <= 19 indicates asthma may be poorly controlled, with an ACT score <= 15 indicating very poor control.

gates.criterion: Asthma symptom control assessed and documented at every review (good control per Appendix 6 classification or ACT >= 20)

steps.description: Commence collaborative care (after eligibility, history, examination, spirometry and symptom control assessment). Optimal management of asthma involves a multidisciplinary and collaborative team-based approach (and as such communication and clinical handover with other care providers is essential).

gates.criterion: Collaborative care with the patient's usual healthcare provider commenced (for Entry Point 1: collaborative management with a medical practitioner established before further program participation)

steps.description: Develop and implement management plan. Non-pharmacological measures (provide to all patients regardless of whether pharmacotherapy is prescribed): trigger avoidance including immunisation status; smoking and/or vaping cessation; weight management; diet and nutrition; physical activity; pulmonary rehabilitation (if applicable). Pharmacotherapy: initial and/or maintenance management of asthma - treatment Levels 1 to 3 as per 2025 Australian Asthma Handbook; inhaler considerations; adjusting pharmacotherapy; management of asthma exacerbations and acute asthma. Each patient with a confirmed diagnosis of asthma on spirometry should have an individualised written Asthma Action Plan (or existing plan updated) using a validated template, plus an accompanying individualised lifestyle prescription (Appendix 7). Refer the patient to their usual healthcare provider with a comprehensive clinical handover if: symptoms are not controlled with treatment consistent with 'recommended' Level 3 pharmacotherapy and they require treatment consistent with Level 4.

gates.criterion: Symptoms controlled with treatment consistent with 'recommended' Level 3 pharmacotherapy (i.e. treatment consistent with Level 4 is not required)
Patient still eligible for the program and collaborative care established

steps.description: Pharmacotherapy for initial and/or maintenance management of asthma must be in accordance with the current online version of the Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory (Maintenance management of asthma in adults and adolescents), considering the pharmacotherapy recommendations in the current online version of the Australian Asthma Handbook; if the two differ, refer to the Australian Asthma Handbook when making clinical decisions. Key considerations: ICS containing medicines are indicated for all adults and adolescents with asthma; short-acting beta2 agonist (SABA) used alone as needed (without ICS containing treatment) should not be recommended or used for the management of asthma, even if symptoms are infrequent; as-needed low-dose budesonide-formoterol ('recommended' Level 1 treatment) is the least intensive treatment option appropriate for adults and adolescents with asthma; long acting beta2 agonists (LABAs) should never be used without ICS in asthma; montelukast no longer has a role in the routine management of asthma in adolescents and adults - pharmacists must not initiate montelukast under the program or prescribe continued montelukast therapy initiated by a specialist or GP (patients prescribed montelukast must be counselled on neuropsychiatric adverse effects and referred to their specialist provider or general practitioner); patients should not commence an 'alternative pathway' of any level of treatment without consultation with a medical practitioner; for patients with predictable EIB, recommend a dose of their rapid-acting bronchodilator 15 minutes before exercise commences; prescribe asthma medicines delivered via inhaler device, not nebulisation (nebulisation is unnecessary, except in some cases of severe acute asthma).

gates.criterion: Prescribing within treatment Levels 1 to 3 ('recommended' pathway) per the current online Therapeutic Guidelines and Australian Asthma Handbook
Combination products include only medicines able to be prescribed under the program

provenance.section_heading: Pharmacotherapy for initial and/or maintenance management of asthma

steps.description: Inhaler considerations: the choice of medicine and inhaler device should consider patient preference and ability to use the device correctly with appropriate training (inspiratory effort required, patient age, inspiratory effort capability, developmental stage, cognition and dexterity, environmental impact); recommend the use of a spacer device with pressurised metered dose inhalers (consider if a face mask is required); minimise the number of inhalers prescribed and the different types of inhaler devices where possible; demonstrate the correct use of the prescribed inhaler device using a placebo inhaler and provide an inhaler-specific checklist; review inhaler technique and adherence, including dispensing history, at every opportunity, even if the same inhaler or device has been used long-term.

Adjusting pharmacotherapy (step up, step down, or switch from 'alternative' pharmacotherapy to 'recommended' treatment) in accordance with the current online Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory (Summary of stepwise maintenance management). Before stepping up: confirm the patient remains eligible for the program; confirm stepping up is appropriate for the presentation; consider common causes of failure to achieve good symptom control (poor adherence, incorrect inhaler technique, trigger exposure, comorbid or alternative diagnoses); if using 'alternative' Level 2 or Level 3 treatment, consider switching to the corresponding 'recommended' Level treatment before considering a dose increase; refer patients to an appropriate healthcare provider for ongoing management if symptoms are not controlled or have worsened on 'recommended' Level 3 treatment. Stepping down: consider stepping down if prescribed Level 2 or Level 3 treatment (by one treatment Level, with review in 4 to 8 weeks, then at 3 months) if good asthma symptom control maintained for 3 months, symptom control at Level 2 or Level 3 achieved in 1 to 2 months, and low risk of exacerbations; stepping down should not be attempted if the person is exposed to triggers or is travelling; do not withdraw ICS containing treatment completely even if symptoms are infrequent and asthma is well controlled.

gates.criterion: Patient remains eligible for the program and stepping up/down is appropriate for the presentation
Symptoms not controlled or worsened on 'recommended' Level 3 treatment is absent (otherwise refer for ongoing management)

steps.description: Confirm management plan is appropriate. Consult the Therapeutic Guidelines, Australian Medicines Handbook, Australian Asthma Handbook and other relevant references to confirm that management is appropriate, including for: suitability of inhaler device(s) selected; contraindications and precautions; drug interactions; lactation status.

gates.criterion: Management appropriate for: inhaler device suitability, contraindications and precautions, drug interactions, lactation status

steps.description: Communicate agreed management plan: provide comprehensive advice (including supporting written information when required) regarding individual product and medicine use (e.g. medication dosing and inhaler technique), how to manage adverse effects, non-pharmacological measures, how to self-manage their asthma, when to seek further care and/or treatment, when to return for clinical review; provide the patient with an individualised written Asthma Action Plan (or update an existing plan) customised to their management regimen.

Collaborative care: provide a copy of the patient's Asthma Action Plan to their usual healthcare provider (and any other relevant health professionals involved in the patient's care). The communication should also include (if appropriate): relevant medical history, results of any spirometry testing conducted, and level of symptom control; changes to existing pharmacotherapy or new pharmacotherapy (including pharmacotherapy for asthma exacerbations); a summary of advice provided to the patient including recommendations for multidisciplinary care and referrals; the next scheduled review appointment. Provide an update to the patient's usual healthcare provider following each occasion of care, including when any changes are made to the patient's management plan.

Clinical review and ongoing collaboration: all patients should undergo regular clinical review. Review within 2 to 3 months of commencement of management and/or initiation of new pharmacotherapy (including when stepping up treatment); within 1 to 2 months after a step down of treatment; after 2 to 3 months of stable pharmacotherapy at treatment Levels 2 to 3; at least once a year if stable; after any asthma exacerbation, including when oral corticosteroids (OCS) are self-initiated (review by a medical practitioner must occur first). At each appointment (scheduled or unscheduled) thoroughly review the patient's ongoing eligibility for the program, symptom control and exacerbations, patient history changes, inhaler technique, potential adverse effects, Asthma Action Plan, pharmacotherapy need, supply until next review, and referrals. Patients may continue to participate providing their condition remains eligible, they wish to remain in the program, and they attend scheduled reviews; refer all patients (with their consent) who are no longer eligible or suitable, or who do not wish to continue, to an appropriate healthcare provider.

gates.criterion: Condition remains eligible to be managed in the program, patient wishes to remain, and patient attends scheduled reviews

diagnosis_pathways.name: Asthma exacerbations and acute asthma - Asthma Action Plan guidance, escalation and pharmacist-initiated prednis(ol)one (pages 17-18)

steps.description: Management and treatment of asthma exacerbations and acute asthma - include in the patient's Asthma Action Plan: how to recognise an asthma exacerbation and acute asthma (Australian Asthma Handbook - Definition and classification of asthma exacerbations); the signs and symptoms that indicate the need for emergency medical care, and how to manage these according to the National Asthma Council Australia's First Aid for Asthma chart and the Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory (Acute asthma - First aid for acute asthma for patients and community members). Risk factors for life-threatening acute asthma include history of severe exacerbation/s, frequent SABA use, co-existing cardiovascular disease and adverse psychosocial or behavioural factors including socioeconomic disadvantage, psychiatric illness, and social isolation.

provenance.section_heading: Management and treatment of asthma exacerbations and acute asthma

steps.description: Patient self-management of asthma exacerbations and acute asthma: include in the patient's Asthma Action Plan guidance on appropriate self-management (severe and life-threatening acute asthma must be managed in an acute care setting). This guidance should include rapid severity assessment and pharmacotherapy as per the Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory (Acute asthma) and Australian Asthma Handbook - Adjusting treatment / Managing acute asthma in adults and adolescents in primary care. Instruct patients to use their rapid-acting bronchodilator as often as needed when symptoms are worsening (i.e. symptoms are more frequent, are recurring after reliever use, or are not promptly relieved). Clearly detail the maximum dose that can be taken at one time and the maximum dose that can be taken in one 24-hour period as per the Australian Asthma Handbook - Medicines Guide.

gates.criterion: Asthma Action Plan in place with clearly detailed maximum dose at one time and maximum dose in one 24-hour period

provenance.section_heading: Patient self-management of asthma exacerbations and acute asthma

steps.description: Provide and dispense a single prescription for up to 5 days treatment of prednis(ol)one up to a maximum dose of 50mg per day with no repeats as part of the patient's written Asthma Action Plan to self-initiate if: symptoms do not improve with escalation of rapid-acting bronchodilator or ICS/formoterol as per Asthma Action Plan over 24 to 48hrs, and immediate review by a medical practitioner is unavailable. Pharmacist-initiated prednis(ol)one prescriptions can only be dispensed in line with an existing Asthma Action Plan for one single occasion in individuals who may come to serious harm due to difficulty accessing unscheduled healthcare (e.g. > 2hrs from healthcare facility). Subsequent prescriptions for stand-by prednis(ol)one can only be provided by a medical practitioner. Advise the patient that prednis(ol)one should only be used if they experience a severe asthma exacerbation as per the above guidance, and not for any other purpose. Prescribe and dispense only the number of tablets required for up to a 5-day course of prednis(ol)one. Do not issue repeats. Factors to consider in determining appropriateness of the prescription include patient age, access to a pharmacy, and ability to self-manage asthma. If a prescription is not provided, provide detailed instructions for when these patients should seek medical review for their worsening asthma. All patients using prednis(ol)one must also be provided with verbal and written materials about harm of OCS dose accumulation over time.

gates.criterion: Existing written Asthma Action Plan in place with prednis(ol)one self-initiation criteria
Symptoms do not improve with escalation of rapid-acting bronchodilator or ICS/formoterol as per Asthma Action Plan over 24 to 48hrs
Immediate review by a medical practitioner is unavailable
Dispensed only once - 'for one single occasion' (subsequent stand-by prescriptions only from a medical practitioner)
Patient may come to serious harm due to difficulty accessing unscheduled healthcare (e.g. > 2hrs from healthcare facility)

provenance.section_heading: Patient self-management of asthma exacerbations and acute asthma

steps.description: Patients who self-initiate prednis(ol)one must be followed by review by medical practitioner within 1 to 2 weeks. Instruct patients that they must arrange medical practitioner review as soon as possible after starting prednis(ol)one (including those with prescriptions from a general practitioner). At this review, the medical practitioner may choose to prescribe further OCS if clinically indicated.

gates.criterion: Patient self-initiated prednis(ol)one

provenance.section_heading: Patient self-management of asthma exacerbations and acute asthma

steps.description: Advise patients to seek emergency care/call an ambulance (even if they have self-initiated prednis(ol)one) if any of: they have severe breathing difficulties; their symptoms get worse very quickly; their rapid-acting bronchodilator has little or no effect; they have difficulty speaking sentences; they experience blue lips or drowsiness; they experience any other signs of severe or life-threatening acute asthma. For more information see the Australian Asthma Handbook - Definition and classification of asthma exacerbations and Managing acute asthma in adults and adolescents in primary care.

gates.criterion: Any of: severe breathing difficulties; symptoms get worse very quickly; rapid-acting bronchodilator has little or no effect; difficulty speaking sentences; blue lips or drowsiness; any other signs of severe or life-threatening acute asthma

steps.description: Advise all patients to return to the pharmacist (or their chosen healthcare provider) for review of their Asthma Action Plan after an asthma exacerbation, even if it was mild and self-managed.

gates.criterion: Asthma exacerbation occurred (even if mild and self-managed)

treatments.dose: up to a maximum dose of 50mg per day
treatments.max_quantity: a single prescription with no repeats; 'Prescribe and dispense only the number of tablets required for up to a 5-day course of prednis(ol)one. Do not issue repeats.'
treatments.quantity_to_supply: only the number of tablets required for up to a 5-day course; no repeats
treatments.notes: Self-initiation supply as part of the patient's written Asthma Action Plan only, if: symptoms do not improve with escalation of rapid-acting bronchodilator or ICS/formoterol as per Asthma Action Plan over 24 to 48hrs, AND immediate review by a medical practitioner is unavailable. 'Pharmacist-initiated prednis(ol)one prescriptions can only be dispensed in line with an existing Asthma Action Plan for one single occasion in individuals who may come to serious harm due to difficulty accessing unscheduled healthcare (e.g. > 2hrs from healthcare facility). Subsequent prescriptions for stand-by prednis(ol)one can only be provided by a medical practitioner.' 'Advise the patient that prednis(ol)one should only be used if they experience a severe asthma exacerbation as per the above guidance, and not for any other purpose.' Factors to consider in determining appropriateness of the prescription include patient age, access to a pharmacy, and ability to self-manage asthma. All patients using prednis(ol)one must be provided with verbal and written materials about harm of OCS dose accumulation over time. Route/strength per tablet not printed beyond the 50mg per day maximum; maximum dose at one time and maximum dose in one 24-hour period are 'as per the Australian Asthma Handbook - Medicines Guide' and are not printed in this document. 'Oral corticosteroids should not be supplied as part of an Asthma Action Plan before spirometry is performed that supports a diagnosis of asthma' (p.11).

provenance.section_heading: Patient self-management of asthma exacerbations and acute asthma

treatments.notes: 'As-needed low-dose budesonide-formoterol ('recommended' Level 1 treatment) is the least intensive treatment option appropriate for adults and adolescents with asthma.' 'Most patients can commence and continue maintenance treatment with as-needed low-dose budesonide-formoterol ('recommended' Level 1 treatment).' No product-level dose, device, route or quantity is printed in this protocol; treatment levels are defined in the Australian Asthma Handbook and Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory. Where pharmacotherapy is prescribed, the patient's prescription(s) (including repeats) should provide enough medicine for the period until the patient's next scheduled review (p.13).

'recommended' Level 3 pharmacotherapy as per the Australian Asthma Handbook, described in this protocol as '(i.e. medium dose Inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)-formoterol maintenance-and-reliever therapy)'. Patients with poor asthma symptom control despite this treatment who require treatment consistent with Level 4 are ineligible (p.4) and must be referred. 'Consider starting treatment with a regimen that includes maintenance ICS (at Level 2 or Level 3) if the patient has frequent or severe symptoms, has had a previous severe exacerbation, or is at high risk of exacerbations.' No product-level dose, device or quantity printed.

provenance.section_heading: Patients who are ineligible for the program

treatments.notes: DO NOT INITIATE UNDER THIS PROGRAM (protocol prohibition, verbatim p.15): 'Montelukast no longer has a role in the routine management of asthma in adolescents and adults. Pharmacists must not initiate montelukast under the program or prescribe continued montelukast therapy initiated by a specialist or GP. Patients should be referred to a medical practitioner for review of ongoing need and prescription before reentering the program.' 'Montelukast is associated with potential neuropsychiatric adverse events. Pharmacists must not initiate montelukast under the program and must not prescribe continued monteleukast therapy initiated by a specialist or GP. Patients prescribed montelukast must be counselled accordingly, see the Therapeutic Goods Administration Safety Update January 2025 and referred to their specialist provider or general practitioner.' 'Counsel relevant patients on the risk of neuropsychiatric adverse effects with montelukast, see the Therapeutic Goods Administration Safety Update January 2025.'

treatments.drug: short-acting beta2 agonist (SABA) used alone as needed (without ICS containing treatment)
treatments.notes: MUST NOT BE USED for asthma management (protocol prohibition, verbatim p.8 and p.15): 'As-needed SABA alone (without ICS) should never be prescribed or recommended to manage asthma. ICS-containing medicines are indicated for all adults and adolescents with asthma.' 'SABA alone (without ICS) used as needed should not be recommended or used for the management of asthma, even if symptoms are infrequent.' Patients 'requiring >=12 short-acting beta2 agonist (SABA) canisters in a year or equivalent over 3 months' require treat-and-concurrently-refer (p.5); SABA use > 2 times per week or >=3 canisters per year is an indication for review by an appropriate healthcare provider (p.19).

treatments.drug: long acting beta2 agonist (LABA) used without ICS
treatments.notes: MUST NOT BE USED without ICS in asthma (protocol prohibition, verbatim p.14): 'Long acting beta2 agonists (LABAs) should never be used without ICS in asthma.'

treatments.dose: a dose of their rapid-acting bronchodilator
treatments.frequency: 15 minutes before exercise commences (for patients with a diagnosis of asthma who experience predictable EIB)
treatments.notes: 'For patients with a diagnosis of asthma who experience predictable EIB, recommend they use a dose of their rapid-acting bronchodilator 15 minutes before exercise commences (see the Australian Asthma Handbook - Exercise and asthma)' (p.15). Separately, 'Instruct patients to use their rapid-acting bronchodilator as often as needed when symptoms are worsening' with the maximum dose at one time and in one 24-hour period detailed 'as per the Australian Asthma Handbook - Medicines Guide' (p.17) - those numeric limits are not printed in this protocol. Patients with EIB but without any other evidence of asthma should be referred to a medical practitioner (p.8).

'ICS containing medicines are indicated for all adults and adolescents with asthma' (p.14); 'All adults and adolescents with asthma should be prescribed ICS' (p.15); 'Do not withdraw ICS containing treatment completely, even if symptoms are infrequent and asthma is well controlled. 'Recommended' Level 1 pharmacotherapy is suitable for most patients with asthma long-term.' (p.16). Doses/devices are defined by the Australian Asthma Handbook treatment levels and are not printed here.

provenance.section_heading: Indications for review by an appropriate healthcare provider

routine: Refer the patient to their usual healthcare provider with a comprehensive clinical handover if the patient is, or becomes, ineligible for management under the program. Ineligibility for treatment as part of a pilot service does not preclude a patient from accessing services provided as part of usual pharmacy care.
Refer when: the patient is aged below 16 or above 65 years (does not preclude a patient from accessing usual pharmacy care); if they are, or become, ineligible for the program.

Treat (if clinically appropriate) and concurrently refer: Provide treatment (if clinically appropriate and concurrently refer) the patient to an appropriate healthcare provider for further review if they: have well controlled type 2 diabetes; have chronic rhinosinusitis or obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA); require >=12 short-acting beta2 agonist (SABA) canisters in a year or equivalent over 3 months; have suspected or confirmed aspirin (or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID)) -exacerbated respiratory disease.

Other referral criteria: Once a patient enters the Improved Asthma Symptom Control Program their eligibility and need for referral may change due to changes in health status, symptoms, or demographic factors. Always ensure the patient is reassessed for eligibility at each consultation. Further referral criteria are included in Indications for review by an appropriate healthcare provider.

Provide a copy of the patient's Asthma Action Plan to their usual healthcare provider (and any other relevant health professionals involved in the patient's care), including medical history, spirometry results, level of symptom control, pharmacotherapy changes, summary of advice and referrals, and the next scheduled review appointment.
Refer all patients (with their consent) who are no longer eligible or suitable for management within the program, or who do not wish to continue in the program, to an appropriate healthcare provider.
urgent: Have any alarm signs and symptoms including haemoptysis, chest pain, unexplained weight loss or gain, night sweats, fever, signs of bronchiectasis, recurrent pneumonia, orthopnoea, or oedema (prompt medical review is required)

Advise the patient to be reviewed by an appropriate healthcare provider as soon as possible if: there is deterioration in their condition; they are needing to use their rapid-acting bronchodilator > 2 times per week or use >=3 canisters per year; their symptoms have not improved after changes to therapy and regular and correct inhaler use after 3 months and ACQ5 remains >= 1.0 or ACT< 20; they experience intolerable adverse effects; they have difficulty using their inhaler device; any alarm signs or symptoms occur; any comorbid conditions become uncontrolled or any new conditions occur that may complicate asthma management or control
emergency: Advise patients to seek emergency care/call an ambulance (even if they have self-initiated prednis(ol)one) if: they have severe breathing difficulties; their symptoms get worse very quickly; their rapid-acting bronchodilator has little or no effect; they have difficulty speaking sentences; they experience blue lips or drowsiness; they experience any other signs of severe or life-threatening acute asthma.

Refer the patient to their usual healthcare provider (or emergency services, if required) with a comprehensive clinical handover if the patient is, or becomes, ineligible for management under the program.

If the patient presents with acute respiratory symptoms that suggest an asthma exacerbation without a previous diagnosis (Entry Point 1), the patient must be referred to their usual healthcare provider (or emergency services, if required) before they can enter the program.

open_questions.topic: Two-column ineligibility list on page 4 - ordering reconstructed
open_questions.observed: Page 4 prints 25 ineligibility bullets across two columns; the flat text extraction interleaves the columns line by line. Columns were reconstructed by x-coordinate (left column first: EXC-1 to EXC-15; right column second: EXC-16 to EXC-25).
open_questions.why_unclear: If the printed reading order is row-wise rather than column-wise, the checklist order differs (the criteria set is unchanged). No criterion text is affected.

open_questions.topic: Ambiguous wording of EXC-5 (suspected respiratory bacterial infection)
open_questions.observed: The bullet reads 'Have a suspected respiratory bacterial infection that requires antibiotic therapy:' followed by the indented sub-bullet '- the patient may continue to be managed in the program (if otherwise appropriate) following concurrent referral to a medical practitioner for review for antibiotic therapy', inside a list titled 'Patients who are ineligible for the program'.
open_questions.why_unclear: It is not stated whether such patients are ineligible (with a permitted continuation), eligible-with-compulsory-referral, or ineligible only when the referral cannot be arranged. Recorded as EXC-5 (confidence medium) plus exception EXE-2.

open_questions.observed: 'Are actively receiving or have previously received within the past 12 months (without required follow-up appointments), specialist treatment for asthma or another respiratory condition (unless they have a written referral from their treating specialist or general practitioner to participate in the program)'.
open_questions.why_unclear: The parenthetical '(without required follow-up appointments)' sits between 'received' and 'specialist treatment'; it is not printed whether it modifies active treatment, past treatment, or follow-up status. Transcribed as printed; exception EXE-3 recorded for the written-referral clause.

open_questions.observed: Inclusion side states 'Patient aged 16 to 65 years'; exclusion side states 'Are aged < 16 years or > 65 years'. Both readings agree that 16 and 65 are inclusive.
open_questions.why_unclear: No ambiguity found; recorded to document that age_bounds 16/65 is the printed pair.

open_questions.topic: Gate on_fail not stated for several pathway gates
open_questions.observed: The document does not state what happens when: consent cannot be documented (PW-1-S2), symptom control is not at target at assessment (PW-1-S11), the management plan is not confirmed appropriate (PW-1-S17), combination products include non-programme medicines (PW-1-S14), or the prednis(ol)one self-initiation criteria are not both met (PW-2-S3, other than 'If a prescription is not provided, provide detailed instructions for when these patients should seek medical review').
open_questions.why_unclear: Spec requires on_fail 'unclear' plus an open question where the document is silent; these are recorded as 'unclear' rather than inferred.

open_questions.topic: No product-level dosing for maintenance pharmacotherapy
open_questions.observed: Treatment Levels 1 to 3, inhaler devices, strengths, doses, frequencies and quantities are not printed; they are delegated to the current online Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory (Maintenance management of asthma in adults and adolescents) and the 2025 Australian Asthma Handbook. Only prednis(ol)one (up to 50mg per day, up to 5 days) carries printed numbers.
open_questions.why_unclear: TX-2, TX-3, TX-5, TX-6, TX-8 therefore have blank dose/strength/quantity fields; nothing can be transcribed without inventing it.

open_questions.topic: Maximum single and 24-hour rapid-acting bronchodilator doses not printed
open_questions.observed: 'Clearly detail the maximum dose that can be taken at one time and the maximum dose that can be taken in one 24-hour period as per the Australian Asthma Handbook - Medicines Guide.'
open_questions.why_unclear: The numeric limits are external to this document, so TX-1/TX-7 max_dose cannot be filled beyond the printed 50mg per day prednis(ol)one cap.

open_questions.observed: Referral destinations and criteria appear on pages 1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9, 11, 18 and 19.
open_questions.why_unclear: Spec allows one shared provenance for the referral block using the first page; first page recorded as 1 with the range noted here.

open_questions.observed: Page 5 lists four criteria under 'Treat (if clinically appropriate) and concurrently refer' with no urgency language; page 4 alarm signs carry '(prompt medical review is required)' and page 18 lists ambulance triggers.
open_questions.why_unclear: Severity for the page 5 criteria was set to 'low' (routine review) because no urgency is printed; alarm signs set to 'high' and ambulance triggers to 'critical' on the document's own wording.

open_questions.topic: No version number or effective date printed
open_questions.observed: Page 30 footer codes read "62'GUA" and "180510-DEC"; the document shows © Department of Health 2026 and references the 2025 Australian Asthma Handbook, but no protocol version/date.
open_questions.why_unclear: instrument_version and effective_date could not be filled from a printed identifier.

open_questions.observed: 'Document informed consent from the patient for participation, as per the Pilot Handbook.' The Pilot Handbook is a separate document.
open_questions.why_unclear: The consent documentation requirements cannot be transcribed from this protocol.

open_questions.observed: Page 17 both provides 'a single prescription ... with no repeats' and states 'Subsequent prescriptions for stand-by prednis(ol)one can only be provided by a medical practitioner', plus a GP-prescription path ('including those with prescriptions from a general practitioner').
open_questions.why_unclear: How a patient obtains a stand-by supply after the single pharmacist occasion (and whether a new Asthma Action Plan is required) is not specified in this document.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Encode treatment Levels 1 to 3 (drug, strength, dose, route, frequency, device) from the current online Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory (Maintenance management of asthma in adults and adolescents) and the 2025 Australian Asthma Handbook before any dosing rule is used - none are printed in this protocol.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: TX-2, TX-3, TX-5, TX-6 and TX-8 have blank dose/strength/quantity fields; a prescribing support module cannot issue supply instructions without the external treatment-level tables.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm the rule for resolving differences between the two source guidelines: 'If the Australian Asthma Handbook and Therapeutic Guidelines differ, refer to the Australian Asthma Handbook when making clinical decisions.'
hugh_to_confirm.reason: This precedence rule drives every pharmacotherapy decision and must be confirmed as the go-live behaviour of the rules engine.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm pharmacist EACPP approval and authorisation status per the Medicines and Poisons Regulations 2016 (WA): 'This document alone does not provide an authorisation for a pharmacist to prescribe.'
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Prescribing under the protocol is conditional on individual Department of Health approval, which is not verifiable from the document.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Obtain the Pilot Handbook consent documentation requirements referenced by 'Document informed consent from the patient for participation, as per the Pilot Handbook.'
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Consent is a gating step (PW-1-S2) but its required content and record format are external to this protocol.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm local process for verifying the prednis(ol)one access criterion 'individuals who may come to serious harm due to difficulty accessing unscheduled healthcare (e.g. > 2hrs from healthcare facility)' and the 'one single occasion' limit.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Both are hard dispensing conditions that must be checked at supply, but the document gives no verification method, distance measurement or register.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm the numeric maximum dose at one time and in one 24-hour period for rapid-acting bronchodilators from the Australian Asthma Handbook - Medicines Guide (not printed here) before encoding maximum-dose checks.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: The protocol instructs pharmacists to detail these limits in the Asthma Action Plan but does not print them.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm spirometry capability requirements for this pharmacy: pharmacist training, appropriate equipment, and quality assurance and audit processes per the National Asthma Council Australia Spirometry Handbook for Primary Care, or the referral alternative for lung function testing.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Whether spirometry can be conducted on site versus referred is a local capability decision that gates Entry Point 1 participation.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm local policy on 'alternative pathway' treatment: 'Patients should not commence an alternative pathway of any level of treatment without consultation with a medical practitioner.'
hugh_to_confirm.reason: The protocol forbids starting alternative-pathway regimens without medical consultation but does not define the consultation/recording process.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm the montelukast handling pathway: counselling content per the TGA Safety Update January 2025 and referral to specialist provider or GP, plus 'review of ongoing need and prescription before reentering the program'.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Montelukast cannot be initiated or continued by the pharmacist; the re-entry/referral workflow is not specified in the document.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm local supply policy for 'the patient's prescription(s) (including repeats) should provide enough medicine for the period until the patient's next scheduled review'.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Quantity-to-supply depends on the local review schedule; no quantity caps are printed in this protocol (unlike other EACPP guidelines that cap total supply).

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm how the program handles pregnant/planning-pregnancy patients and patients aged < 16 or > 65 (all ineligible) in the rules engine: referral destination and whether usual pharmacy care advice is auto-issued.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: The document requires a comprehensive clinical handover to the usual healthcare provider but does not specify destination, timing or scripted advice.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Confirm which review timeframe applies when several overlap (e.g. step up plus exacerbation): the document lists within 2 to 3 months, within 1 to 2 months after step down, after 2 to 3 months stable at Levels 2-3, at least once a year if stable, and 1 to 2 weeks after self-initiated prednis(ol)one, noting 'shorter review periods may be clinically necessary'.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Precedence between overlapping review intervals is left to clinical judgement and must be decided locally.
